summary: Explains how IGMPv3 and MLDv2 let hosts tell neighboring routers they want to receive multicast traffic, and how they support source-specific multicast, where a host asks for traffic from a particular sender. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Source-specific multicast lets a viewer ask for one particular sender inside a multicast group, instead of everything anyone sends to that group. This RFC says how the two group membership protocols, IGMP for IPv4 and MLD for IPv6, must behave when the group address is in the range reserved for that service.

questions: what is the ssm address range
subtitle: How the group membership protocols handle a request for one specific source inside a multicast group.

tldr.problem: IGMP version 3 and MLD version 2 let a host ask for traffic from named sources inside a multicast group, but neither says what those protocols should do when the group address belongs to the source-specific multicast range.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines what an SSM-aware host and an SSM-aware router do with each message type for an SSM address: EXCLUDE records are refused, older-version reports are ignored, and every other record and query follows the normal rules.
tldr.outcome: Source-specific multicast works over IPv4 and IPv6 with the existing group management protocols, and a router cannot be pushed back into older behaviour by another host on the same link.

facts.label: Group records used for an SSM address

today: RFC 4604 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 3376 and RFC 3810 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated, so the rules it sets for the source-specific range still stand.

sections.title: What the Document Adds
sections.content:
The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) lets an IPv4 host tell its neighbouring routers which IP multicast groups it belongs to. IGMP version 3 adds the ability for a host to ask for traffic from individual sources inside a multicast group, or to filter those sources out. The Multicast Listener Discovery Protocol (MLD) offers the same function for IPv6 hosts, and MLD version 2 adds the same source filtering to MLD.

Because the two protocols do the same job, the document refers to them together as group management protocols, and to the source-filtering versions of them as source filtering group management protocols.

Source-specific multicast needs only small changes to those protocols on hosts and routers. RFC 4607 sets out the general requirements that a system implementing the source-specific multicast service model has to follow. This document applies those requirements to systems that implement IGMPv3 and MLDv2. It defines modifications to the host and router parts of IGMPv3 and MLDv2, and it clarifies how those protocols behave when the address is a source-specific one. The document updates the IGMPv3 and MLDv2 specifications, and any protocol change it makes is marked with the tag MODIFICATION so that a reader can tell a change from a clarification.
sections.plainLanguage: IGMP and MLD are the protocols a computer uses to tell its nearby routers which multicast channels it wants. Version 3 of IGMP and version 2 of MLD let the computer name the sources it wants. This RFC says what those two protocols must do when the channel address belongs to the range reserved for source-specific multicast.

sections.title: The Source-Specific Address Range
sections.content:
The 232/8 IPv4 address range is allocated by IANA for source-specific multicast. In IPv6, the FF3x::/32 range, where x is a valid IPv6 multicast scope value, is reserved for source-specific multicast semantics, and the allocations made today are restricted to FF3x::/96. A host that knows the source-specific address range and can apply source-specific semantics to it is called an SSM-aware host.

A host or router may be configured to apply source-specific semantics to addresses outside the range allocated by IANA. The group management module should have a configuration option that sets the source-specific address range, and if it has one it must default to the range allocated by IANA. The mechanism for setting the option must at least allow manual configuration; a protocol to set it may be defined later.
sections.plainLanguage: Source-specific multicast uses a reserved block of addresses: 232/8 in IPv4 and the FF3x::/32 range in IPv6, with today's allocations inside FF3x::/96. A device that knows this block and applies the source-specific rules to it is called SSM-aware. The block can be configured by hand, and when it is, it must start from the allocated range.

sections.title: What an Application Is Told
sections.content:
If the host IP module of an SSM-aware host receives a request to receive multicast traffic sent to a source-specific destination address, but the request is not source-specific, the module should return an error to the application, as specified in RFC 3678. This is a modification to the socket interface described in that document.

On a host that is not SSM-aware, an application that uses the wrong kind of request, for example a plain join of the group or a request that excludes a source, will not receive the service it asked for. An SSM-aware router, following the rules of this document, refuses to process that request, and the application gets no indication of the problem beyond the traffic never arriving.

The document also makes clear how much of this matters. Source-specific multicast can be used by any host that supports the source filtering APIs and whose operating system supports the appropriate group management protocol. The modifications described in this document make source-specific multicast work better on an SSM-aware host, but they are not strict prerequisites for using it.
sections.plainLanguage: An application on an SSM-aware host that asks for a whole group instead of one source gets an error back. On an ordinary host the same request fails silently, because the router refuses it and the application only notices that the traffic never arrives.

sections.title: What an SSM-Aware Host Does
sections.content:
For reports, the document separates the old versions from the new. An SSM-aware host operating under IGMPv3 or MLDv2 could send an IGMPv1, IGMPv2 or MLDv1 report for a source-specific address while it is in older-version compatibility mode. That is an exceptional condition, meaning the routers cannot provide the source filtering the host needs, and the host logs an error when it enters that mode for such an address. In that situation the traffic sent to a channel is unlikely to reach a host that asked for it. IGMPv3 and MLDv2 allow a host to let an older-version report suppress its own membership record, but an SSM-aware host must not allow that in this situation, because suppressing reports would give an attacker a way to deny the service to other hosts on the link.

A host may report more than one source-specific channel in a single report, either by listing several sources inside one group record or by sending several group records. A group record for a source-specific address may be a MODE_IS_INCLUDE record as part of a current-state record, an ALLOW_NEW_SOURCES record as part of a state-change record, or a BLOCK_OLD_SOURCES record as part of a state-change record. A report may carry source-specific and any-source multicast addresses at the same time. A CHANGE_TO_INCLUDE_MODE record may also be sent, for instance when the source-specific address range is changed through configuration, and a router should process it by the normal rules. An SSM-aware host should not send MODE_IS_EXCLUDE or CHANGE_TO_EXCLUDE_MODE records for a source-specific address, because exclude mode does not apply to those addresses.

For queries, the behaviour differs by type. An IGMPv1 query, or an IGMPv2 or MLDv1 general query, makes the host fall back to the older mode of operation on that interface: it stops reporting source-specific subscriptions and starts reporting interest in all source-specific addresses without naming a source, so the router stops applying source-specific semantics to that group. A host should log an error when it receives such a query for a source-specific address. An IGMPv2 or MLDv1 group specific query for an address in any configured source-specific range is processed normally, and the host should log an error, since such a query suggests that the sending router is either not compliant with this document or is configured with a different range.

An IGMPv3 or MLDv2 group-specific query for a source-specific address must be answered with a report if the group matches the source-specific destination address of any of the host's subscribed channels. The document notes that a router has no reason to send such a query today, but that its meaning is well defined in that range and future implementations may have reason to send one, so the host should be liberal in what it accepts.

A group-and-source-specific query must be answered when the group and the source in the query match a channel the host subscribes to, and the host must be able to handle a query that lists several sources per group. Using a source-specific address does not change either of those rules. IGMPv2 leave and MLDv1 done messages are not processed by hosts, and should not be sent for a source-specific address unless the host has fallen back to older-version compatibility mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The host sends source-specific records for a source-specific address: include, allow new sources, or block old sources. It must not send the exclude records, because exclude does not apply to these addresses, and it must not let an old-style report hide its own report, since that would let someone on the same link cut off the service. An old-style general query makes the host fall back to reporting whole groups.

sections.title: Keeping a Shared Network Consistent
sections.content:
The case where a host falls back to older-version behaviour needs an operational answer. An IGMPv1 query, or an IGMPv2 or MLDv1 general query, makes the host revert to the older mode on that interface, which stops it reporting source-specific subscriptions and makes the router stop applying source-specific semantics to the group address.

A router that complies with this document would never send an IGMPv1, IGMPv2 or MLDv1 query for an address in the source-specific range. So this situation arises only when the router is not SSM-aware, or when the host and the router disagree about the source-specific address range, for instance because they were configured by hand and the configurations do not match.

To reduce the problem, the document says it must be administratively assured that all routers on a given shared-medium network comply with this document and agree about the source-specific address range.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts fall back to the old behaviour only if a router sends an old-style query, which a compliant router never does for these addresses. So the fallback points to a configuration mismatch on the shared network, and the fix is to make sure every router on that network agrees about which addresses are source-specific.

sections.title: What an SSM-Aware Router Does
sections.content:
A router has to know the source-specific address range to provide the source-specific service model, and a router that knows the range and can apply the semantics to it is called an SSM-aware router. It may have a configuration option that applies the semantics to addresses outside the allocated range, and if it has one, it must default to the allocated range.

For reports, a router should ignore a MODE_IS_EXCLUDE current-state record or a CHANGE_TO_EXCLUDE_MODE filter-mode-change record when it refers to a source-specific address, and it may log an error. It must process the other group records in the same report. A CHANGE_TO_INCLUDE_MODE filter-mode-change record is processed by the normal rules. An IGMPv1, IGMPv2 or MLDv1 report for an address in the source-specific range could come from a host that is not SSM-aware, and the router should ignore all such reports and specifically should not use them to establish IP forwarding state. It may log an error.

For queries, general queries are sent periodically with no change in behaviour for source-specific multicast. Group-specific queries for addresses in the source-specific range are not prohibited, although a router conforming to IGMPv3 or MLDv2 would not send one today. Group-and-source-specific queries are used when a receiver has said it is no longer interested in a particular source and group pair, in order to find out whether any directly attached hosts still are. They are sent normally, as the group management specifications require.

Two cases complete the rules. A router that loses the querier election to a router running a lower version must log an error, as the group management specifications already require. And an IGMPv2 leave or MLDv1 done message for an address in the source-specific range, which could come from a host that is not SSM-aware, should be ignored, and the router may log an error.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that supports source-specific multicast refuses the records that do not apply to it, namely the exclude records, and ignores reports from hosts running older versions of the protocols so that it never builds forwarding state from them. The other records and queries are handled exactly as before.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol modifications in this document are not known to create any security concerns beyond those already present when IGMPv3 or MLDv2 is used with any-source multicast. The document refers the reader to RFC 4607 for an analysis of the security issues specific to source-specific multicast.

One point is called out as important. A router must not accept non-source-specific reception requests for a source-specific destination address. The rules of IGMPv3 and MLDv2 require a router, on receiving such a membership report, to fall back to older-version compatibility mode for the group in question. If the router did fall back in this situation, it would stop an IGMPv3-capable host on the link from receiving the source-specific service for that address, which would create the possibility of an attacker denying that service to other hosts on the same link.
sections.plainLanguage: The changes in this RFC do not add new security problems of their own. The one point to watch is that a router must keep ignoring requests that do not name a source, because falling back to the old behaviour would let anyone on the link cut off the service for everybody else.

viz.caption: WHAT AN SSM-AWARE ROUTER DOES WITH EACH MESSAGE

items.title: Exclude records
items.text: Ignored for a source-specific address, and the rest of the report is still processed.

items.title: Older-version reports
items.text: Ignored, and never used to set up forwarding state.

items.title: General query
items.text: Sent as usual, with no change for source-specific multicast.

items.title: Group-specific query
items.text: Allowed in the source-specific range, although it is not sent today.

items.title: Group-and-source query
items.text: Used to check whether other hosts still want a source and group pair.
